Q: Does JavaScript support array/list comprehensions like Python? A:

Given the question's Python code

print([int(i) for i in str(string) if i not in forbidden])

this is the most direct translation to JavaScript (ES2015):

const string = '1234-5';
const forbidden = '-';

console.log([...string].filter(c => !forbidden.includes(c)).map(c => parseInt(c)));
// result: [ 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ]

Here is a comparison of the Python and JavaScript code elements being used: (Python -> Javascript):

  • print -> console.log
  • unpacking string to list -> spread operator
  • list comprehension if -> Array.filter
  • list comprehension for -> Array.map
  • substr in str? -> string.includes

Q: Calculate dates of two different records in case statement A:

Compare TRINT5 to the TRINT2 date, not to itself.

SELECT DISTINCT 
  Inc.ID,
  Acuity.translation AS Acuity,
  CT.contactd AS ContactDate,
  CT.ContType AS ContactType,
  CT.CreateDate,
   CASE
     WHEN Acuity.translation = 'Family Consult to Start'
       AND CT.ContType = 'TRINT5'
       AND CT.contactd >= T2.TRINT2Date
       AND CT.contactd <= DATEADD(DAY, 3, T2.TRINT2Date)
     THEN 'Met'
      ELSE 'Not Met'
   END AS MetNotMet
FROM dbo.MC_CDCPIncident AS Inc
LEFT JOIN dbo.MC_CDCPContactNotes AS CT 
   ON CT.MC_CDCPIncident = Inc.id
LEFT JOIN dbo.validation_list_values AS Acuity 
   ON Inc.echono_c = Acuity.value 
  AND Acuity.validation_list_id = '60158CDD-199D-4E6E-B339-E2B4E40D72BE'
OUTER APPLY
(
  SELECT MIN(CT2.contactd) AS TRINT2Date
  FROM dbo.MC_CDCPContactNotes AS CT2
  WHERE CT2.MC_CDCPIncident = Inc.id
    AND CT2.ContType = 'TRINT2'
) AS T2
WHERE Inc.id = '20260127044748623E81DED612F96420CBA9';

Q: Tracking visited nodes when traversing datastructure A:

Keeping the ids of visited nodes in a set is fine -- as long as you don't delete any.

ids are only unique for objects that exist at the same time, so if you delete a node and create a new one, it could have the same id as the deleted node.

Q: Validate Index for a Collection A:

I have a hard time to really understand your underlying requirement. As you know, you can access an entry of a collection either via index or via key. The index is an (long) integer, the key is a string (and always as string).

Using the index can be used to iterate over the collection. There might be cases where you know that a specific entry is on a specific index (e.g. you know that the main sheet of an Excel workbook is on index 1, but already that might fail). What you for sure never will have is the requirement to access an element by index and have a Double holding that index. If you have a situation like that, you have a design flaw. If, in any situation, you want to calculate the index of an entry from an floating number (eg "use index 1 for values between 0 and 1), the calling code must do this calculation, not any library function.

Using keys means that the calling code needs to know the key. If you have a date as key, the calling code needs to convert it into a unique string (maybe by using the Format-function), both when creating entry and when retrieving it. Don't implement such logic into a library function - you never know if the user needs an entry per day, per month, per hour...

(As you maybe already noticed, accessing an entry via key is magnitude faster than by index)

So your code should accept only (long) integer values and strings, everything else is an error. Don't do any magic conversations or let VBA do any implicit conversations for you.

Check the VarType of the variable. Assume that you are dealing with an index only if you have a vbInteger or a vbLong data type. Assume that you are dealing with an key only if you have a vbString data type. Throw an error (or whatever is needed in your case) for any other data type as they are not valid.

Some remarks to the edge case you have listed:

Platform: Dealing with integers as index and strings as keys is for sure compatible between operating systems. And as mentioned, all others point to a basic design flaw.

Numeric text: Is a string and not a number, so is will be uses as key, not as index. Quick prove:

Dim c As New Collection
c.Add "First element", "2"
c.Add "Second element", "1"
Debug.Print c(1), c("1")

prints

First element Second element

Numeric interpretation: There is no such thing as to interpret anything. A number is a number, a string is a string.

Numeric conversion: No need to convert anything. Especially the conversion from Empty to 0 you mentioned makes absolutely no sense.

Scientific notation: No such thing. Notation is a way to represent a number (on the screen or a printout or a text file). A Long (or Double) stores a number in an internal binary format, no matter if you display it as 1000 or 1e4. However, the string "1000" is something completely different as the string "1e4", and both are different from the numeric value 1000.

Rounding: Again, don't use any other numerical data type except integers as index, especially not if it holds fractions. If you need an entry for 3.14, convert it to a string and use it as key, not as an index.

Dates: The fact that dates are stored as Doubles internally doesn't qualify then as index. Side note: If you would use the day part (CLng(now)) as index, you first needs to make sure that for every date since 1.1.1900 an entry in your collection would exist. If you really want to access entries by date, convert them into a string explicitly, but that means you have a key, not an index.

Overlarge numbers: Firstly, this is not a real world problem - except if you have a collection with more than 2 billion entries. Anyhow, just to let you know, the following code will work:

Dim d As Double, c as New collection
d = 2147483647# * 2
If d > c.Count Then Debug.Print "Not in list"

Booleans: The fact that they are represented in VB* as integers doesn't qualify them as index.

Default members: An object doesn't qualify neither as index nor as key. That is also true for Uninitialized objects (Nothing).

If you are dealing with any data type that isn't an integer or a string, throw an error. Don't go down the rabbit hole "I don't want to bother the user with errors and therefore do all possible conversions silently" - it will just lead to errors that are hard to find.

Q: How can I find reasons why an udev rule is not applied? A:

For the udev rule /ect/udev/rules.d/99-bizrfid.rules I would add the SUBSYSTEM:

ACTION=="add", SUBSYSTEM=="tty", ATTRS{idVendor}=="09d8", ATTRS{idProduct}=="0420", SYMLINK+="ttyMyDevice"

You could add also ATTRS{manufacturer}==, but idVendor and idProduct are sufficient.

Otherwise it looks correct and the test run creates the symlink:

creating link '/dev/ttyMyDevice' to '/dev/ttyACM0'

Q: How to find Inverse Modulus of a number i.e (a%m) when m is not prime A:

All you need to pre-assert is that the moduli are co-prime. If you knew the totient of the moduli, or preferably, the reduced totient (aka carmichael-lambda) of the moduli, ahead of time, and the moduli themselves are manageable in size, you can directly solve for x without dealing with the extended Euclidean algorithm at all.

It works even when the values haven't been pre-reduced to its modulo form, and best illustrated by an example. Say this pair of inputs :

x ≡  47 (mod 40)
x ≡ 139 (mod 63)

Their modulo form would be :

x ≡   7 (mod 40)
x ≡  13 (mod 63)

The exponent for the inverse is simply 1 less than the reduced-totient (this relationship is true for both primes and composites) :

𝛌(40 := 2^3 x 5) := 4  | InvExpn(40) := 𝛌(40) - 1 := 3
𝛌(63 := 3^2 x 7) := 6  | InvExpn(63) := 𝛌(63) - 1 := 5

Putting it together, and the consolidated (and highly symmetric) arithmetic expression to obtain x would simply be :

jot -w "$( mawk 'BEGIN {

    print ( (63 % 40)^3 % 40 *  47 * 63 \
          + (40 % 63)^5 % 63 * 139 * 40 ) % (63 * 40) 

}' ) %% %u => _5_" 9 | mawk '$5 = ($1 % $3)_' | rs -t -c$'\n' -C 0 3

2407 % 1 => 0   2407 % 4 => 3   2407 % 7 => 6
2407 % 2 => 1   2407 % 5 => 2   2407 % 8 => 7
2407 % 3 => 1   2407 % 6 => 1   2407 % 9 => 4

You can also combine the reduction to modulo form step with that of obtaining the modulus' inverse :

( (63 % 40)^3 *  47 % 40 * 63 \
+ (40 % 63)^5 * 139 % 63 * 40 ) % (63 * 40) => 2407

And technically, if you already knew the totient / reduced totient, and pre-asserted the co-primality of the moduli, you wouldn't even need to invert anything, and can directly get back x with just 1 single modulo-(%)-op :

( 63^4 *  47 \                                              
+ 40^6 * 139 ) % (63 * 40) => 2407

Two other tricks can help save time (or even bypass the entire process altogether) :

  1. Group absolute modulos together by the LCM of all their moduli. The classic Chinese Remainder Theorem example
x ≡ 2 (mod 3)
x ≡ 3 (mod 5)
x ≡ 2 (mod 7)

is really only 2 equations to solve, not 3 :

x ≡ 3 (mod  5)
x ≡ 2 (mod 21)

Which you can verify using the consolidated expression :

( (3 * 7)^4 * 3 \
 +   5^(12) * 2 ) % (3 * 5 * 7) => 23   # using totients

( (3 * 7)^4 * 3 \
 +   5^( 6) * 2 ) % (3 * 5 * 7) => 23   # using reduced-totients

2. Group by relative shortfalls by the LCM of all their moduli. So this seemingly chaotic set of 3 congruences with 3 prime moduli and 3 remainders that are themselves prime ….

x ≡ 19 (mod 23)
x ≡ 43 (mod 47)
x ≡ 67 (mod 71)

…. is really just 1 single congruence that stipulates nothing more than a subtraction, no inversion needed whatsoever :

x ≡ -4 (mod 76751 = 23 * 47 * 71)

x = 76751 - 4
  = 76747

jot -w '76747 %% %u =>' 71 | 
              awk '$3 ~ /23|47|71/ { print $0, $1 % $3 }'

76747 % 23 => 19
76747 % 47 => 43
76747 % 71 => 67

At times, totients of prime components of a composite modulus has a LOT of overlap, the computational cost to calculate the inverse favors binary exponentiation over the extended GCD :

m := 10,813,280,829,486,135 = 3 5 7 11 13 19 31 37 41 61 73 181

𝛟(m) := 3482851737600000 | InvExpn(m) := 𝛟(m)-1 := 3,482,851,737,599,999
     
     := 5 * 8^7 * 9^6 

𝛌(m) := 360              | InvExpn(m) := 𝛌(m)-1 := 359

     := 5 * 8 * 9

To obtain 65537's inverse of 3453511467445478 (mod 10813280829486135), the boiler plate extended GCD algorithm needed 11 modulo-(%)-ops (and another 11 corresponding div-(/)-ops), for a total of 22 high-cost div-or-mod ops. Some inputs can go over 20 mods only.

On the other hand, 359 only has 9-bits, so even when using a non-branching always-multiply variant of modular exponentiation, the theoretical max is only 18 modulo-(%)-ops (and 0 div-(/)-ops).
